newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Banks,telecoms firms spend more to advertise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Banks,telecoms firms spend more to advertise.

text.p: Advertisements for breakfast cereals, soft drinks and washing powder have traditionally dominated British television, but a new breed of advertisers with multi-million-pound budgets is beginning to make an impact, industry experts say.

They say banks and telecommunications groups are running expensive advertising campaigns as they battle for market share, while so-called "fast moving consumer goods" (FMCG) companies are doing less advertising.

"Financial services and telecommunications companies are beginning to spend serious money on advertising while some FMCG suppliers are cutting back their advertising budgets," Martin Jones, managing director of the Advertising Agency Register, which matches ad agencies with potential clients, told Reuters recently.

One of the biggest of the non-traditional advertisers is British Telecommunications Plc, which last year spent an estimated 100 million pounds ($163.3 million) on its "good to talk" promotion campaign.
"There is a shift in the advertising marketplace," Gary Duckworth, chairman of ad agency Duckworth Finn Grubb Waters, told Reuters.

"FMCG brands still account for a significant share of advertising expenditure, but in the long term their share is diminishing as the newer kinds of brand owner use advertising as an important weapon in the competitive armoury," he said.
He said financial services and telecommunications companies were realising that high-profile advertising was a good way to build brand awareness and to target consumers.
"They realise that the strength of a brand can make a real difference in markets that are becoming more hard-fought, more fast-moving and more turbulent," he said.
Meanwhile some traditional advertisers such as food and drink companies are moving to other forms of promotion including direct mail.

Deborah Morrison, director of member services at the Incorporated Society of British Advertisers, said, "They are not necessarily cutting their spend, but are refocusing it to look at things such as direct marketing and customer loyalty programmes to maximise their opportunities to communicate with consumers."
Some companies are also advertising fewer of the brands in their portfolios.

"The trend is for traditional advertisers to put money behind fewer brands because it takes such serious money to make an impact amongst the clutter of television advertising," said Jones from the Advertising Agency Register.
These new types of advertisers often have to send more complex messages to their target audience than food and drink companies.
"A bank, for example, will operate in a variety of markets -- mortgages, loans, current accounts -- and will normally target businesses as well as consumers, homeowners and students," said Duckworth.
"So advertising is given a broader set of rules to play," he said.
